title: Scope in linear vs iterative projects
blurb: Contrast fixed scope with change control against prioritised, flexing scope using MoSCoW.
question: A charity must launch a fundraising app before its winter appeal, on a fixed budget, but nobody is sure which features donors will value most. Should its scope be fixed up front and controlled, or prioritised and allowed to flex? And what does each choice mean for time and cost?

teach.body: Every project manages scope: it identifies, defines and controls what will be delivered. What changes between life cycles is WHEN the scope is pinned down and WHAT is allowed to give when reality bites. A linear project fixes the scope early and lets time and cost flex. An iterative project fixes time and cost and lets the scope flex, delivering the most valuable things first.

teach.h: What is fixed, and what flexes?
teach.caption: Exam shorthand: linear fixes SCOPE; iterative fixes TIME and COST, so scope is what gives.

teach.body: In a linear life cycle the scope is defined in detail and baselined early, in the definition phase, then controlled through formal change control. Any request to alter it is an exception: captured, assessed for impact and approved, rejected or deferred. Example: Northgate Council's new footbridge. The design, span and load rating are agreed before construction, and a request to widen it mid-build goes through change control, with time and cost adjusted if approved.

teach.h: Scope through a linear life cycle

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: Scope defined in detail and baselined

teach.body: In an iterative life cycle the scope is defined at a high level and refined as the team learns. Requirements sit in a prioritised backlog, owned by the product owner. Each time box has fixed time and cost; the team builds the highest-priority items first. New ideas are not 'changes to a baseline' but new backlog items, absorbed by re-prioritising between iterations. Example: the charity's fundraising app, where donor feedback after each release reshapes what comes next.

letters.sub: Essential: without it the solution does not work
Important, but the solution still works without it
Desirable: the first to drop if time runs short
Agreed out of this release, may return later

teach.caption: The lower-case o's are only there to make the word pronounceable.

teach.h: Linear vs iterative scope at a glance

teach.text: Classic distractor: 'in an iterative project, scope and quality are fixed'. Wrong. In iterative working it is TIME and COST that are fixed, and SCOPE that flexes. Also, 'Won't have' means won't have THIS TIME, not rejected forever. And iterative does not mean uncontrolled: scope is still managed, through prioritisation.

items: Linear: scope defined in detail and baselined in definition, then protected by formal change control.
Linear: scope is fixed, so time and cost may flex to deliver it.
Iterative: scope defined at a high level and refined; time and cost are fixed and scope flexes.
Iterative: requirements prioritised with MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time).
Iterative: change is absorbed by re-prioritising the backlog between iterations.

summary: You can now explain how scope is fixed and protected by change control in a linear project, and how it is prioritised and allowed to flex within fixed time and cost in an iterative one. You can also expand MoSCoW and say which requirements give way first.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, in which phase is the scope normally defined in detail and baselined?
A.why: In a linear life cycle, the definition phase sets out the requirements in detail and establishes the baseline, before deployment starts.

whyNot.0: Deployment is where the work is done; by then the scope baseline should already be agreed.
whyNot.1: Transition hands the outputs over; it is far too late to define scope.
whyNot.3: Adoption belongs to the extended life cycle after transition, when outputs are already in use.

A.q: In an iterative project, which elements are normally fixed?
A.why: Iterative working fixes time and cost (per time box) and lets the scope flex, delivering the highest priorities first.

whyNot.0: This is the classic distractor: scope is the element that flexes in iterative working.
whyNot.2: Time is fixed, but scope is not; scope is what gives.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed, but scope is not; scope is what gives.

A.q: In MoSCoW prioritisation, what does the W stand for?
A.why: W is 'Won't have this time': requirements agreed to be outside the current release, which may be reconsidered later.

whyNot.0: 'Would like to have' is a common misremembering; the category is 'Won't have this time'.
whyNot.1: There is no 'worth doing later' category; deferred items are 'Won't have this time'.
whyNot.2: Sponsor wishes are not a MoSCoW category; priority depends on business value, not who asked.

B.q: On a linear project, the client asks to alter a deliverable that is already in the approved scope. How should this be handled?
options: By the team at a daily stand-up
By dropping a Could have item
B.why: In linear projects the scope is baselined, so any change to it must be captured, assessed and decided through formal change control.

whyNot.1: Re-prioritising a backlog is how iterative projects absorb change, not linear ones.
whyNot.2: The delivery team cannot change an approved baseline informally; that would be scope creep.
whyNot.3: Dropping Could haves is an iterative technique for protecting a fixed deadline.

B.q: On an iterative project, a promising new requirement emerges after the second iteration. How is it normally accommodated?
options: The end date moves to fit it in
It is prioritised in the backlog
The budget is raised to pay for it
B.why: New requirements are added to the backlog and prioritised against everything else; lower priorities give way if needed.

whyNot.0: Time is fixed in iterative working, so the end date does not move to absorb scope.
whyNot.1: Emerging requirements are expected in iterative working; there is no need to restart.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed in iterative working, so the budget does not grow to absorb scope.

B.q: Which statement about 'Must have' requirements is correct?
options: Delivered only if there is time
Without them it does not work
B.why: Must haves are essential: without them the solution would not work or would not be usable, so they are delivered first.

whyNot.0: Doing something only if time allows describes a Could have.
whyNot.1: Deferring to a later release describes a Won't have this time.
whyNot.2: Optional extras are Could haves, not Must haves.

C.q: A charity must launch a fundraising website before a fixed campaign date, on a fixed budget, but its exact features are unclear. Which approach to scope suits it best?
options: Linear, with the date allowed to slip
Iterative, with time and cost flexing
C.why: Fixed time and cost with uncertain requirements is exactly where iterative scope management fits: prioritise with MoSCoW and let scope flex.

whyNot.1: Fixing every feature up front is risky when the requirements are unclear.
whyNot.2: The campaign date is fixed, so an approach that lets the date slip does not fit.
whyNot.3: In iterative working time and cost are fixed; it is scope that flexes.

C.q:
Which TWO statements describe scope management on a linear project?
1. Scope is defined in detail early on
2. Time and cost may flex to deliver the scope
3. Scope is re-prioritised each time box
4. Time and cost are fixed while scope flexes
C.why: Linear projects fix the scope early in detail, so time and cost are the elements that may flex to deliver it.

whyNot.0: Statement 3 describes iterative working, where scope is re-prioritised each time box.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 describes iterative working, where time and cost are fixed.
whyNot.3: Both statements 3 and 4 describe iterative, not linear, scope management.

C.q: Near the end of a time box, the team realises not every planned requirement will be finished. In iterative scope management, what normally happens?
options: The time box end date is moved
Extra budget is found to finish
Quality checks are skipped to finish
C.why: Time and cost are fixed, so scope gives: lower-priority items (Could haves first) are deferred to a later time box.

whyNot.0: The end of a time box does not move; that is the point of time boxing.
whyNot.2: Cost is fixed in iterative working, so extra budget is not the answer.
whyNot.3: In a time box it is scope that is adjusted; skipping quality checks risks outputs that are not fit for purpose.

reteach.title: A fitted kitchen vs a wedding day
reteach.question: Picture two projects: a fitted kitchen built exactly to a signed-off design, and a wedding with a fixed date and a fixed budget. Where does scope give in each one?

blocks.h: Two ways to protect a project
blocks.body: The kitchen is linear. Units, worktops and appliances are chosen and signed off before the fitters arrive. Change your mind about the worktop and the fitter writes up a change, with a new price and date: the scope is fixed and time and cost give. The wedding is iterative. The date and budget cannot move, so you prioritise. The venue and registrar are Must haves, a band is a Should have, a chocolate fountain a Could have, fireworks a Won't have this time. If money runs short, the fountain goes.

blocks.text: If the date and the budget are fixed, scope must be the thing that flexes. That is the iterative pattern the exam looks for.

explain.body: Defined in detail and baselined in the definition phase. From then on, changes are exceptions handled by formal change control. Scope is fixed; time and cost may flex to deliver it. Suits stable, well-understood requirements.

test.q: Which phrase best describes scope on a linear project?
test.why: Linear scope is defined in detail and baselined early, then controlled through formal change control.

whyNot.0: Loose, evolving scope describes iterative working.
whyNot.1: Re-prioritising each cycle describes iterative working.
whyNot.3: Scope is fixed in definition, before deployment starts, not after it.

explain.body: Defined at a high level, then refined. Requirements live in a prioritised backlog, owned and prioritised by the product owner. Time and cost are fixed per time box; scope flexes. Change is absorbed by re-prioritising between iterations.

test.q: On an iterative project, who normally owns and prioritises the backlog of requirements?
test.why: The product owner represents the business and users, and owns and prioritises the product backlog.

whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case and benefits, but does not prioritise the backlog day to day.
whyNot.2: The PMO supports projects with standards and assurance; it does not own requirements.
whyNot.3: The governance board gives direction and decisions at gates, not backlog prioritisation.

explain.body: Must have (essential), Should have (important, but it works without), Could have (desirable, first to drop), Won't have this time (agreed out of this release). When a fixed deadline is under threat, priorities are protected from the top down.

test.q: A 'Could have' requirement is best described as one that is:
options: essential for the solution to work
important, but not vital this release
agreed to be outside this release
desirable, and first to drop if late
test.why: Could haves are desirable but less important, so they are the first to be dropped if time runs short.

whyNot.1: Important but not vital requirements are Should haves.
whyNot.2: Requirements agreed to be outside this release are Won't have this time.

explain.body: Stable, well-understood requirements and a need for certainty about what will be delivered point to linear scope management. Uncertain or emerging requirements, with a fixed date or budget, point to iterative scope management.

children.label: Iterative
children.sub: Fix time and cost, flex scope

test.q: Which project is best suited to linear scope management?
options: An app shaped by ongoing user feedback
A bridge built to a fixed design
A trial of a new online service
test.why: A bridge built to an agreed, stable design has well-understood requirements, so fixing scope early and controlling change suits it.

whyNot.0: Features shaped by feedback are emerging requirements, which suit iterative working.
whyNot.2: A trial is about learning as you go, which suits iterative working.
whyNot.3: Unclear features are emerging requirements, which suit iterative working.
